quotes.t: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
Write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year.
The creation of a thousand forests is in one acorn.
New beginnings are available to all of us over fifty times a year; they are called Mondays.
It isn't always easy to apologize for your mistakes but doing so shows a person with a strong sense of self.

Good memories are most often created without conscious effort. These are the memories that result from those unselfish acts or behaviors that give of our time, talents or gifts without any due regard for repayment.
Your conscience is the measure of the honesty of your selfishness. Listen to it carefully.
The bond that links your true family is not one of blood, but of respect and joy in each other's life.
Heaven is not a place, and it is not a time. Heaven is being perfect.
Where ignorance is our master, there is no possibility of real peace.
Calm mind brings inner strength and self-confidence, so that's very important for good health.
Love and compassion are necessities, not luxuries. Without them, humanity cannot survive.
Peace is the result of retraining your mind to process life as it is, rather than as you think it should be.
I am realistic – I expect miracles.
The fact that you are willing to say, 'I do not understand, and it is fine,' is the greatest understanding you could exhibit.
Patience, persistence and perspiration make an unbeatable combination for success.
It is literally true that you can succeed best and quickest by helping others to succeed.
The best way to sell yourself to others is first to sell the others to yourself.
Do not worry about your difficulties in mathematics. I can assure you mine are still greater.
God does not play dice with the universe.
I know not with what weapons World War III will be fought, but World War IV will be fought with sticks and stones.
If you want to improve, be content to be thought foolish and stupid.
The greater the difficulty, the more glory in surmounting it. Skillful pilots gain their reputation from storms and tempests.
Whoever does not regard what he has as most ample wealth, is unhappy, though he be master of the world.
Listen to the reed, how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.
How many flee from one calamity into another; how many leap from the snake towards the dragon.
Why do you stay in prison, when the door is so wide open?
Our doubts are traitors, and make us lose the good we oft might win, by fearing to attempt.
Neither a borrower nor a lender be.
There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
Think of yourself as dead. You have lived your life. Now, take what's left and live it properly.
Be tolerant with others and strict with yourself.
Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
There are those who give with joy, and that joy is their reward.
When you reach the end of what you should know, you will be at the beginning of what you should sense.
Sadness is but a wall between two gardens.
You must love in such a way that the person you love feels free.
Understanding someone's suffering is the best gift you can give another person. Understanding is love's other name. If you don't understand, you can't love.
Every breath we take, every step we make, can be filled with peace, joy and serenity.
He who cannot draw on three thousand years is living from hand to mouth.
Daring ideas are like chessmen moved forward. They may be beaten, but they may start a winning game.
What is the hardest of all? That which seems easiest for your eyes: to see with your eyes what is before your eyes.
We come nearest to the great when we are great in humility.
Do not say, 'It is morning,' and dismiss it with a name of yesterday. See it for the first time as a new-born child that has no name.
Life is given to us, we earn it by giving it.
Let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it.
The dogmas of the quiet past are inadequate to the stormy present.
We shall nobly save, or meanly lose, the last best hope of earth.
Research your own experience, absorb what is useful, reject what is useless, add what is essentially your own.
The successful warrior is the average man, with laser-like focus.
Simplicity is the key to brilliance.
Difficulties strengthen the mind, as labor does the body.
The whole future lies in uncertainty: live immediately.
We learn not in school, but in life.
The roots of education are bitter, but the fruit is sweet.
All human actions have one or more of these seven causes: chance, nature, compulsions, habit, reason, passion, desire.
Youth is easily deceived because it is quick to hope.
I have never let my schooling interfere with my education.
Get your facts first, and then you can distort them as much as you please.
The human race has one really effective weapon, and that is laughter.
The only impossible journey is the one you never begin.
One does not become enlightened by imagining figures of light, but by making the darkness conscious.
An eye for an eye will only make the whole world blind.
Supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting.
From one thing, know ten thousand things.
Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.
Never give in, never give in, never, never, never, never — in nothing, great or small, large or petty.
You did in your twenties what you knew how to do, and when you knew better you did better.
What we have once enjoyed we can never lose. All that we love deeply becomes a part of us.
They alone live who live for others.
The biggest adventure you can take is to live the life of your dreams.
Thinking is the capital, Enterprise is the way, Hard Work is the solution.
Spread love everywhere you go. Let no one ever come to you without leaving happier.
We are generally the better persuaded by the reasons we discover ourselves than by those given to us by others.
Do what you feel in your heart to be right — for you'll be criticized anyway.
Success is the child of audacity.
The chief enemy of creativity is good sense.
Poor is the pupil who does not surpass his master.
Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.
Love is the answer, and you know that for sure; Love is a flower, you've got to let it grow.
There are two tragedies in life. One is to lose your heart's desire. The other is to gain it.
The supreme happiness of life is the conviction that we are loved; loved for ourselves — say rather, loved in spite of ourselves.
The evil that is in the world comes almost always from ignorance.
And we should consider every day lost on which we have not danced at least once.
All men make mistakes, but a good man yields when he knows his course is wrong, and repairs the evil. The only crime is pride.
Hunger makes thief of any man.
To serve is beautiful, but only if it is done with joy and a whole heart and a free mind.
We all have self-doubt. You don't deny it, but you also don't capitulate to it.
For most of history, man has had to fight nature to survive; in this century he is beginning to realize that, in order to survive, he must protect it.
You're only given a little spark of madness. You mustn't lose it.
Born a wildlife warrior, die a wildlife warrior.
I won't be a rock star. I will be a legend.
The Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves.
The most dangerous phrase in the language is, 'We've always done it this way.'
There are three ways to ultimate success: The first way is to be kind. The second way is to be kind. The third way is to be kind.
The most sophisticated people I know – inside they are all children.
We don't make mistakes, just happy little accidents.
With every drop of water you drink, every breath you take, you're connected to the sea. No matter where on Earth you live.
People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it.
Creating a life that reflects your values and satisfies your soul is a rare achievement.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Abraham Lincoln.bio: 16th president of the United States (1861-1865), who led the country through the Civil War and abolished slavery.

Ada Lovelace.bio: English mathematician (1815–1852), who wrote the first algorithm intended to be processed by a machine.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Einstein.bio: German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theory of relativity, one of the pillars of modern physics. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.
Albert Einstein.credit: Photograph by Orren Jack Turner, Princeton, N.J. Modified with Photoshop by PM_Poon and later by Dantadd., Public domain (File: Albert Einstein Head.jpg)

Aristotle.bio: Greek philosopher and student of Plato; founder of logic and many scientific fields.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Bill Watterson.bio: American comic artist (born 1958), creator of the Calvin and Hobbes comic strip.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Bob Ross.bio: American painter (1942–1995), host of the television series The Joy of Painting.

Bruce Lee.bio: Bruce Lee was a Hong Kong-American martial artist and actor who transformed martial-arts cinema with films such as Enter the Dragon. His philosophy of adaptability — 'be water' — blended Taoist ideas with his own Jeet Kune Do.
Bruce Lee.credit: National General Pictures, Public domain (File: File:Bruce Lee 1971 National General Pictures publicity photo.jpg)

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.
Carl Jung.credit: AnonymousUnknown author, Public domain (File: File:CARL JUNG (1875 - 1961).jpg)

Dalai Lama.bio: The 14th Dalai Lama, spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1989), based in Dharamshala, India.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Epictetus.bio: Epictetus was a Greek-born slave in Rome who won his freedom and became one of the most influential Stoic teachers. His Discourses and the handbook known as the Enchiridion teach that freedom lies in mastering one's own judgments and desires.

Fred Rogers.bio: American television host (1928–2003) of the children's program Mister Rogers' Neighborhood.

Freddie Mercury.bio: British singer and songwriter (1946–1991), lead vocalist of the band Queen.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Grace Hopper.bio: American computer scientist and U.S. Navy rear admiral (1906–1992), a pioneer of the COBOL programming language.

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Jacques Cousteau.bio: French naval officer and explorer (1910–1997), pioneer of underwater filmmaking and co-inventor of the Aqua-Lung.

Jim Henson.bio: American puppeteer (1936–1990), creator of the Muppets.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a German writer, poet, playwright and natural philosopher, regarded as Germany's greatest literary figure. His works include the drama Faust, The Sorrows of Young Werther and Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.credit: Joseph Karl Stieler, Public domain (File: Goethe (Stieler 1828).jpg)

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Kahlil Gibran.bio: Lebanese-American writer and poet, best known for The Prophet (1923), one of the best-selling books of all time.

Kobe Bryant.bio: American basketball player (1978–2020), 20 seasons with the Los Angeles Lakers and five-time NBA champion.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Marcus Aurelius.bio: Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher, author of the Meditations.

Mark Twain.bio: American writer (Samuel Clemens) known for Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Hill.bio: Napoleon Hill was an American self-help author best known for Think and Grow Rich (1937), one of the best-selling books of its kind. His work popularized the idea that success follows from definite purpose and a positive mental attitude.
Napoleon Hill.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Napoleon Hill headshot.jpg)

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pearl S. Buck.bio: German-born American physicist (1879–1955), the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

Rabindranath Tagore.bio: Bengali poet and polymath from India; the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913), known for Gitanjali.

Ralph Waldo Emerson.bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson was an American essayist and philosopher who led the Transcendentalist movement, arguing for self-reliance, intuition and the spiritual presence in nature. His essays 'Nature' and 'Self-Reliance' shaped American thought, and he mentored both Thoreau and Whitman.
Ralph Waldo Emerson.credit: Albert Southworth, Public domain (File: File:Daguerreotype of Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1846.jpg)

Richard Bach.bio: Richard Bach is an American writer best known for the bestselling novella Jonathan Livingston Seagull (1970) and Illusions (1977). A former Air Force pilot, his work often combines flying with spiritual themes.
Richard Bach.credit: Corsair133693, CC BY-SA 3.0 (File: File:Von Richthofen LYNN GARRISON - DICK BACH.jpg)

Robin Williams.bio: American actor and comedian (1951–2014), star of Dead Poets Society and Mrs. Doubtfire.

Rumi.bio: 13th-century Persian poet and Sufi mystic whose Masnavi is among the most influential works of Islamic literature.

Seneca.bio: Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman, author of Letters to Lucilius.

Simon Sinek.bio: British-American author and speaker (born 1973), known for the book Start With Why and his 2009 TEDx talk on inspirational leadership.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Irwin.bio: Australian wildlife expert and television presenter (1962–2006), host of The Crocodile Hunter.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Sylvia Earle.bio: American marine biologist and oceanographer (born 1935), known as 'Her Deepness'.

Thich Nhat Hanh.bio: Vietnamese Buddhist monk and peace activist who popularized mindfulness in the West; nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr.
Thich Nhat Hanh.credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 (File: File:Hòa thượng Ấn Kim - Tổ Tuân - Hoằng Tịnh. 印 金 祖 恂 弘 净.jpg)

Tony Robbins.bio: Tony Robbins is an American author, coach and motivational speaker known for bestselling books such as Unlimited Power and Awaken the Giant Within. His seminars and self-help programmes have made him one of the most prominent figures in the personal development industry.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Wayne Dyer.bio: Wayne Dyer was an American self-help author and motivational speaker whose first book, Your Erroneous Zones (1976), became one of the best-selling books of all time. He wrote more than forty books and lectured widely on self-development and spirituality.

William Shakespeare.bio: English playwright and poet, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language; author of Hamlet and Macbeth.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
